summary: At 35.7 square miles, La Quinta sprawls larger than the city of San Francisco, yet holds fewer than 40,000 residents — a striking ratio that tells you almost everything about the landscape before you arrive. The city sits at the base of the Santa Rosa Mountains in the eastern Coachella Valley, and that geography delivers dramatic sunset alpenglow against rugged desert peaks to the west while morning light floods in across the open valley floor. With an annual average of 10.5 hours of sunshine per day and a mean high of 84°F, summer heat is genuinely punishing — triple-digit stretches are routine from June through September — but winters are the payoff, delivering warm, dry days that explain the area's deep ties to golf and resort tourism. The local economy leans heavily on hospitality, healthcare, and service-sector employment anchored to the broader Palm Springs metro; this is less a standalone job center than a residential base where many commute along Interstate 10 or Highway 111. A median home price around $613,000 against a median household income near $97,600 produces a price-to-income ratio of roughly 6.3:1, comfortable compared to coastal California but still requiring substantial purchasing power. The built environment is largely master-planned subdivisions separated by wide desert boulevards, with the La Quinta Cove area nestled closest to the mountains offering trail access into the Santa Rosas — but day-to-day errands almost universally require a car. La Quinta is a place whose identity is inseparable from its extreme climate: spectacular for roughly seven months, endurance-tested for the other five.
